lesson.grammar_point: phrasal verbs as a system: separable, inseparable and intransitive

vocab.title: Match each phrasal verb to its meaning
defs: to check something carefully, step by step
to play a recording again so you can listen to it
to make a sound slowly quieter until it stops
to prepare equipment so it is ready to use
to move something to a later time
to stop working suddenly, usually a machine
to think of an idea or a plan

paras: The session was booked for ten, so the assistant engineer arrived at eight to set everything up. She set up the microphones for the drums, checked every cable and set the headphones up for the band. By half past nine, the room was ready, and nobody had to wait.

The first take was too loud in the headphones, so the singer asked the engineer to turn the band down. He turned it down a little, and they recorded the first verse again. Then they played it back in the control room. It sounded clean, but the producer was not happy with the start of the song. "It's too slow," she said. "We need something different." During the coffee break, the guitarist came up with a new intro: four bars, only guitar and voice.

Then, in the middle of the third take, the old mixing desk broke down. There was no sound at all. For a moment, everybody looked at the engineer. He did not panic. He went over every connection, one by one, and twenty minutes later he sorted it out: one cable was loose. The band wanted to carry on, but the singer's voice was tired. So the producer made a decision. They put the vocal off until Thursday and carried on with the instruments.

At six, they went over the plan for Thursday and played the best take back one last time. There was one more question. Should the song stop on the last chorus, or should they fade it out? They decided to fade it out slowly, over twenty seconds. It was a long day, but the song was in better shape than in the morning.

items.situation: The bass is too loud in your headphones. Ask the engineer to do something about it.
tips: Can you turn the bass down a little?
Separable: with it, the pronoun goes in the middle -- turn it down.

items.situation: You just recorded a take. Suggest listening to it again.
tips: The pronoun goes in the middle. Never play back it.

items.situation: A colleague asks what you do before a session starts. Tell her.
tips: I set up the microphones and check the cables.
Set up the microphones = set the microphones up.

items.situation: The producer asks why the vocal is not recorded yet. Explain.
tips: The singer was tired, so we put it off until Thursday.
Put off = move to a later time.

items.situation: Tell your teacher how you usually come up with ideas for a song or a show.
tips: I usually come up with ideas when I'm walking or driving.
Three words, and they never separate: come up with.

items.situation: Something broke down at work this year. Say what it was and who sorted it out.
tips: The computer in the edit room broke down, and the tech team sorted it out in an hour.
No object after break down. Sort it out: the pronoun goes in the middle.

listenings.text: I am a sound engineer on a live music show, and Saturday is the day that matters. We get to the studio at noon and set up the stage: twelve microphones, two drum kits and a piano. At four, we have the sound check. Each band plays one song, and we play it back in the control room to check the balance. Last week, one singer said her voice was too loud in her ear monitor, so I turned it down, and she was happy. Then, one hour before we went live, a wireless microphone broke down. There was no time to repair it, so we went over the plan again and gave her a spare one. The show is live, so we can't put anything off. If something goes wrong during the show, we carry on, and we sort it out in the break. Nobody at home ever knows.

People always ask me how I come up with ideas for songs. Honestly, it is not magic. It is a system. Every morning, I record one minute of anything: a melody, a beat, a sentence. I don't judge it. I just save it and carry on with my day. On Fridays, I go over everything I recorded that week. I play each idea back once, and most of them are terrible. That's fine. Maybe one is interesting, and I keep that one. My biggest problem was always putting things off. I used to say, I will start the song next week, and next week never came. Now I have a rule. If an idea is good, I work on it the same day, even for ten minutes. And when a song doesn't work, I don't throw it away. I take it back to voice and guitar, and very often it comes back to life.
